title: Symmetric and Hermitian Matrices: the Spectral Theorem

intro.x: General matrices can have complex eigenvalues, missing eigenvectors and badly conditioned eigenvector bases. Symmetric matrices have none of these problems. Their eigenvalues are real, their eigenvectors can be chosen orthonormal, and they are always diagonalisable by an orthogonal change of basis. This is the spectral theorem, arguably the most important theorem in applied linear algebra: it underlies principal component analysis, vibration modes, the second-derivative test, covariance estimation, and the SVD of the next chapters.

blocks.x: Throughout, a real matrix is symmetric if $A\T=A$. The complex analogue is a Hermitian matrix, $A\herm=A$, where $A\herm=\overline{A}\T$ is the conjugate transpose. A real symmetric matrix is Hermitian, so we prove statements for Hermitian matrices and obtain the real case as a special case. Recall that on $\C^n$ the inner product is $\ip{\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{y}\herm\mathbf{x}$.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Eigenvalues of Hermitian matrices are real

blocks.x: If $A=A\herm$ and $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf{0}$, then $\lambda\in\R$.

Compute $\mathbf{v}\herm A\mathbf{v}$ in two ways. It equals $\lambda\mathbf{v}\herm\mathbf{v}=\lambda\norm{\mathbf{v}}^2$. Its conjugate is $(\mathbf{v}\herm A\mathbf{v})\herm=\mathbf{v}\herm A\herm\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}\herm A\mathbf{v}$, so $\mathbf{v}\herm A\mathbf{v}$ is real. Hence $\lambda=\mathbf{v}\herm A\mathbf{v}/\norm{\mathbf{v}}^2$ is real.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal

blocks.x: If $A=A\herm$, $A\mathbf{u}=\lambda\mathbf{u}$, $A\mathbf{v}=\mu\mathbf{v}$ and $\lambda\ne\mu$, then $\mathbf{u}\perp\mathbf{v}$.

$\lambda\ip{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{v}}=\ip{A\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{v}}=\ip{\mathbf{u}}{A\mathbf{v}}=\mu\ip{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{v}}$ (using $A=A\herm$ and that $\mu$ is real). So $(\lambda-\mu)\ip{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{v}}=0$, giving $\ip{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{v}}=0$.
This already shows that eigenspaces of a symmetric matrix for different eigenvalues are mutually perpendicular, which is stronger than the mere independence guaranteed for general matrices.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices

blocks.x: If $A\in\R^{n\times n}$ is symmetric, there is an orthogonal matrix $Q$ and a real diagonal matrix $\Lambda=\diag(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ with
A=Q\Lambda Q\T.

The columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_n$ of $Q$ form an orthonormal basis of $\R^n$ consisting of eigenvectors, $A\mathbf{q}_i=\lambda_i\mathbf{q}_i$. Conversely, every matrix of the form $Q\Lambda Q\T$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $\Lambda$ real diagonal is symmetric.

Induction on $n$. For $n=1$ there is nothing to prove. For $n>1$: the characteristic polynomial has a root $\lambda_1$ over $\C$, which is real by Theorem 15.1, and the real matrix $A-\lambda_1I$ is singular, so there is a real unit vector $\mathbf{q}_1$ with $A\mathbf{q}_1=\lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1$. Let $W=\mathbf{q}_1^\perp$, an $(n-1)$-dimensional subspace. It is $A$-invariant: if $\mathbf{x}\perp\mathbf{q}_1$ then $\ip{A\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{q}_1}=\ip{\mathbf{x}}{A\mathbf{q}_1}=\lambda_1\ip{\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{q}_1}=0$. Choose an orthonormal basis of $W$ and let $U$ be the $n\times(n-1)$ matrix with these columns; then $B=U\T AU$ is a symmetric $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix representing $A|_W$. By induction $B=Q'\Lambda'Q'{}\T$ with $Q'$ orthogonal. Setting $Q=[\mathbf{q}_1\ \ UQ']$, which has orthonormal columns, gives $Q\T AQ=\diag(\lambda_1,\Lambda')$. The converse: $(Q\Lambda Q\T)\T=Q\Lambda\T Q\T=Q\Lambda Q\T$.
The same proof (with $Q$ unitary and the conjugate transpose) shows that every Hermitian matrix is $A=Q\Lambda Q\herm$ with $Q$ unitary and $\Lambda$ real. There is an even more general version.

A complex matrix $A$ is normal ($AA\herm=A\herm A$) if and only if it is unitarily diagonalisable: $A=Q\Lambda Q\herm$ with $Q$ unitary and $\Lambda$ diagonal (possibly complex). Normal matrices include Hermitian ($A\herm=A$), skew-Hermitian ($A\herm=-A$) and unitary ($A\herm A=I$) matrices, and real symmetric, skew-symmetric and orthogonal matrices.

Every matrix has a Schur form $A=UTU\herm$ with $U$ unitary and $T$ upper triangular. If $A$ is normal then so is $T$; comparing the $(1,1)$ entries of $TT\herm$ and $T\herm T$ forces the first row of $T$ to vanish off the diagonal, and inductively $T$ is diagonal. The converse is immediate since diagonal matrices commute with their adjoints.
Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&2\end{pmatrix}$. The characteristic polynomial factors as $(\lambda-2)(\lambda^2-4\lambda+2)$ with roots $2,\ 2\pm\sqrt2$. Unit eigenvectors:
\lambda=2:\ \tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,0,-1);\quad\lambda=2+\sqrt2:\ \tfrac12(1,-\sqrt2,1);\quad\lambda=2-\sqrt2:\ \tfrac12(1,\sqrt2,1).
They are mutually orthogonal (the eigenvalues are distinct), so $Q$ built from them is orthogonal and $A=Q\diag(2,2+\sqrt2,2-\sqrt2)Q\T$. A check: $\tr A=6=2+(2+\sqrt2)+(2-\sqrt2)$.

When an eigenvalue is repeated, its eigenspace has dimension equal to the multiplicity (symmetric matrices are never defective), but any orthonormal basis of that eigenspace is valid; the orthogonal matrix $Q$ is not unique. Gram–Schmidt (Chapter 11) within the eigenspace produces an orthonormal basis. Orthogonality between different eigenspaces is automatic by Theorem 15.2.
The spectral decomposition as a sum of projections
Multiplying out $Q\Lambda Q\T$ using the outer-product view gives
A=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\,\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i\T.

Each $\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i\T$ is the orthogonal projection onto the line through $\mathbf{q}_i$ (Chapter 12). Grouping equal eigenvalues, $A=\sum_\mu\mu P_\mu$ where $P_\mu$ is the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace for $\mu$, and the $P_\mu$ satisfy $P_\mu P_
u=0$ for $\mu
e
u$ and $\sum P_\mu=I$. This is the form that generalises to self-adjoint operators on infinite-dimensional spaces.

For any function $f$ defined on the eigenvalues, $f(A)=Q\,f(\Lambda)\,Q\T=\sum f(\lambda_i)\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i\T$. In particular $A^k=Q\Lambda^kQ\T$, $A^{-1}=Q\Lambda^{-1}Q\T$ if all $\lambda_i\ne0$, $e^A=Qe^\Lambda Q\T$, and if all $\lambda_i\ge0$ then $A^{1/2}=Q\Lambda^{1/2}Q\T$ is a symmetric square root.

Let $A$ be symmetric positive definite and consider the ellipse $\{\mathbf{x}\in\R^2:\mathbf{x}\T A\mathbf{x}=1\}$. Changing to the eigenbasis, $\mathbf{x}=Q\mathbf{y}$, gives $\mathbf{x}\T A\mathbf{x}=\lambda_1y_1^2+\lambda_2y_2^2$ (the orthogonal change preserves lengths). So the ellipse has its axes along the eigenvectors, with semi-axis lengths $1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}$.

blocks.caption: The level set $\mathbf{x}\T A\mathbf{x}=1$ of a positive definite quadratic form is an ellipse whose principal axes are the eigenvectors; the longest axis belongs to the smallest eigenvalue.

sections.title: The Rayleigh quotient and extremal eigenvalues

blocks.x: For symmetric $A$ and $\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}$, $R_A(\mathbf{x})=\dfrac{\mathbf{x}\T A\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{x}}$.
Let $\lambda_{1}\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$ be the eigenvalues of symmetric $A$ with orthonormal eigenvectors $\mathbf{q}_i$. Then
\lambda_1=\max_{\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}}R_A(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\lambda_n=\min_{\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}}R_A(\mathbf{x}),
the maximum and minimum being attained exactly at eigenvectors for $\lambda_1,\lambda_n$. More generally $\lambda_k=\max\{R_A(\mathbf{x}):\mathbf{x}\perp\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_{k-1}\}$.

Write $\mathbf{x}=\sum y_i\mathbf{q}_i$; then $\mathbf{x}\T A\mathbf{x}=\sum\lambda_iy_i^2$ and $\mathbf{x}\T\mathbf{x}=\sum y_i^2$. So $R_A(\mathbf{x})$ is a weighted average of the $\lambda_i$ with weights $y_i^2/\sum y_j^2\ge0$ summing to $1$; it therefore lies between $\lambda_n$ and $\lambda_1$, and equals $\lambda_1$ only if all weight sits on the eigenvectors of $\lambda_1$. Restricting to $\mathbf{x}\perp\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_{k-1}$ sets $y_1=\dots=y_{k-1}=0$, and the same argument gives $\lambda_k$.

The direction of maximum variance of centred data with covariance matrix $\Sigma$ is $\arg\max\mathbf{u}\T\Sigma\mathbf{u}/\mathbf{u}\T\mathbf{u}$, the top eigenvector of $\Sigma$; the variance along it is $\lambda_1$. The second principal component maximises the quotient subject to orthogonality to the first, and so on: the eigenvectors of $\Sigma$ in decreasing order of eigenvalue. This is Theorem 15.8 verbatim, and it is why PCA reduces to an eigendecomposition (or SVD) of the covariance.

For symmetric $A,B$ with eigenvalues ordered decreasingly, $\lambda_k(A)+\lambda_n(B)\le\lambda_k(A+B)\le\lambda_k(A)+\lambda_1(B)$. In particular eigenvalues of symmetric matrices move by at most $\norm{E}_2$ under a perturbation $E$: $\abs{\lambda_k(A+E)-\lambda_k(A)}\le\norm{E}_2$.
This is the quantitative statement that eigenvalues of symmetric matrices are perfectly well-conditioned, in contrast to the non-normal case (Chapter 13).
Two symmetric matrices $A,B$ commute ($AB=BA$) if and only if they have a common orthonormal eigenbasis, i.e. $A=Q\Lambda_AQ\T$ and $B=Q\Lambda_BQ\T$ for one orthogonal $Q$.

If $A,B$ share $Q$, they commute because diagonal matrices do. Conversely let $E$ be an eigenspace of $A$ for $\lambda$. For $\mathbf{x}\in E$, $A(B\mathbf{x})=BA\mathbf{x}=\lambda B\mathbf{x}$, so $B$ maps $E$ into itself, and $B|_E$ is symmetric; apply the spectral theorem to it to pick an orthonormal basis of $E$ of eigenvectors of $B$. Eigenspaces of $A$ for different eigenvalues are orthogonal, so the union of the bases is an orthonormal eigenbasis of both.
Symmetric (Hermitian) matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues.
Spectral theorem: $A=Q\Lambda Q\T=\sum\lambda_i\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i\T$ with $Q$ orthogonal; no defective matrices; the proof is induction using the invariant subspace $\mathbf{q}_1^\perp$.
Normal matrices are exactly the unitarily diagonalisable ones.
Functions of symmetric matrices act on the eigenvalues: $f(A)=Qf(\Lambda)Q\T$.
$\lambda_{\max}=\max R_A(\mathbf{x})$, $\lambda_{\min}=\min R_A(\mathbf{x})$ (Rayleigh–Ritz), the basis of PCA.
